records.content: The Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 11,145 confirmed cases and 5437 confirmed deaths as of November 10, 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). 1 DRC accounts for 11,114 of those cases and 5433 deaths. The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record and is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks, CDC reports. 1 Outside DRC, Kenya has reported 9 confirmed cases and 2 deaths, Uganda 20 confirmed cases and 2 deaths plus 1 probable case and 1 probable death, and Nigeria and France 1 confirmed case each. 1 No cases tied to this outbreak have been reported in the US, and CDC considers the overall risk to the American public and travelers low. 1 Confirmed deaths represent about 49% of confirmed cases. Investigation of additional cases is ongoing, and suspected cases and deaths in DRC are temporarily excluded from the count pending data standardization, so totals are expected to change. 1 The outbreak surpassed 1000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. 1 By comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1000 cases. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC. 1 Cases have been confirmed in the DRC provinces of Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), Nord-Ubangi (North Ubangi), and Tshopo. 1 South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Bundibugyo virus is a type of Ebola virus and the cause of the 2026 outbreak in DRC. CDC reports it is the virus driving cases in DRC, Kenya, and Nigeria. Have any Ebola cases been reported in the US during this outbreak? No. As of November 13, 2026, CDC reports no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak in the US and considers the risk to the American public low. What travel restrictions are in place? Travelers who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight cannot board commercial flights to the US. Travelers from Uganda or South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. As of October 23, Kenya's Ministry of Health has confirmed 9 cases of Ebola disease and 2 deaths. 1 The initial case, reported October 6, involved a man who traveled from DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he was hospitalized and died in an isolation unit. Subsequent cases, including the second death, occurred among relatives and health care providers in close contact with him, all of whom were already in quarantine when diagnosed. 1 Kenya's Ministry of Health has reported no community spread, and all cases were in Nairobi. 1 On October 20, Nigeria reported its first case in the 2026 outbreak, with testing confirming Bundibugyo virus. 1 Uganda reported cases at the same time DRC declared the outbreak, with 21 confirmed and probable cases and 3 deaths overall. 1 The last confirmed case in Uganda recovered and was released from care on July 16, 2026, and France's single patient was released on July 4. 1 Neither country has reported active cases. US entry for travelers recently in DRC remains temporarily restricted. 1 Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight cannot board commercial flights to the US. US citizens and nationals who have been in Uganda or South Sudan, but not DRC, within 21 days of arrival must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. 1 Since 11:59 PM Eastern Standard Time on November 3, all passengers boarding an international flight to the US must attest they have not been in DRC during the 21 days before departure. 1 CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces. Approximately 500 CDC staff are involved in the response, including more than 120 people deployed to affected countries. 1 CDC cites limited health infrastructure, ongoing conflict, and frequent cross-border population movement as barriers to containment. 1 Violence against health care workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to infections among health care workers treating patients. Mistrust of government and misinformation further complicate outreach. 1 For US clinicians, CDC directs providers to its clinical guidance for Ebola disease, screening and diagnosis resources for viral hemorrhagic fevers, and infection prevention and control recommendations for US hospitals. 1 A travel history covering the prior 21 days remains central to identifying patients at risk. Issued on: 16/11/2026 - 20:51 4 min Reading time A port health official checks travellers' information at a health screening station at Murtala Muhammed International Airport following reports of an Ebola case in Nigeria, Lagos, Nigeria, on 22 October, 2026. © REUTERS - Sodiq Adelakun By: RFI Advertising Read more Officially declared on 15 May, the Ebola epidemic affecting the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has continued to spread, reaching eight provinces across the country six months after it first emerged in Ituri. "We are all in agreement today to say that this outbreak is still serious, and is still not under control," Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), said on Sunday. In an interview with RFI, he described the outbreak as "extremely serious". More than 11,200 infections and 5,500 deaths have been reported, according to government data. More than 80 percent of new cases are being detected among people who were not on contact-tracing lists, while over 65 percent of deaths occur in communities rather than healthcare facilities, Kaseya said. Ebola is most contagious during the late stages of the disease. "If we don't stop this outbreak now, it will be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have," he warned. A health worker wears full gear at a Ebola treatment camp in Butembo, Congo, Wednesday, on 30 September, 2026. © AP Photo/Sebastien Kitsa Musayi While research into treatments and vaccines is progressing, efforts to contain the outbreak on the ground continue to face major obstacles. Driven by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, the epidemic is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, after the 2014–2016 outbreak in West Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000. Inside Bunia’s fight to protect families from DRC’s deadliest Ebola outbreak Regional concerns The outbreak has also spread beyond the DRC over the past six months, reaching Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. "Uganda has managed to bring the epidemic under control," Kaseya explained. "We had declared its end there – even though two cases, one from Kenya and one from Nigeria, had passed through Uganda." The situation in Kenya has also improved. Last week, the country announced that the final patient had been discharged from facilities used to monitor people who had come into contact with infected individuals. "We have also seen very good results in Nigeria," Kaseya added. "Not all the identified cases tested positive; at present, the situation appears to be under control." However, the Africa CDC chief remains concerned about the continuing spread of the epidemic within the DRC and the risk of further cross-border transmission. "First, there is the Central African Republic, which is a major source of concern for me. Second, there is South Sudan, which also remains a major source of concern." He also highlighted the potential risk to Rwanda and Burundi if the outbreak spreads from the Beni-Butembo area towards Goma and Bukavu. "And, of course, there are all the other countries that could be affected indirectly," he added. Medical charity warns funding for DRC Ebola fight not reaching front lines Hope for a vaccine Kaseya told RFI that the lack of an effective vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain remains one of the biggest challenges. A vaccine "should have been available for the past 19 years, given that the Bundibugyo strain has been known for that long," he said. He added that the absence of treatments and diagnostic tests specifically designed for the strain had contributed to the scale of the epidemic. Research into treatments and vaccines is progressing, however, with several clinical trials already underway, according to RFI's correspondent in Kinshasa, Paulina Zidi. The "Tumaini" clinical trial – named after the Swahili word for "hope" – is focusing on vaccine development. A group of experts from the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended adding two new vaccine candidates specifically developed to target the Bundibugyo virus. Meanwhile, the Ebo-Pep trial is examining whether the oral antiviral drug obeldesivir can prevent the disease from developing in people exposed to the virus. The trial is being conducted at several locations, including treatment centres in Ituri managed by the medical NGO Alima. Africa CDC chief warns ‘no country is safe’ as Ebola reaches Nigeria Challenges on the ground Instability in eastern DRC, large-scale population movements and weaknesses in healthcare and disease surveillance have all contributed to the scale of the outbreak. Around $2.9 billion has been pledged internationally to help fight the epidemic. However, despite these commitments, much-needed assistance is still failing to reach some of the worst-affected areas, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned last week. The organisation highlighted shortages of trained staff, ambulances without fuel and a lack of surveillance teams. Kaseya acknowledged that coordination between the Congolese government and international donors remains a problem. "We are not pointing fingers," he said. "We are saying it's a collective failure." He called on donors to release around $1.6 billion in pledged aid and work more closely with Kinshasa to ensure funds are used effectively and resources are not wasted through duplication. Kaseya also acknowledged that some healthcare workers had not been paid for months, adding that the Congolese government was working to digitise its payroll system to address the problem.
